description:
Human space exploration is transitioning from temporary orbital missions to permanent interplanetary settlement. Historical analysis indicates that no frontier is sustained arbitrarily; survival demands codified protocols and disciplined knowledge systems. Beyond extreme radiation and ambient vacuum, the most critical hazard in deep space is cognitive latency—the operational paralysis induced when communication delays decouple a crew from terrestrial assistance.
In my view, our team functions to bridge complex aerospace telemetry with human decision-making.
summary:
"MARSWALK is a real-time cognitive lifeline for Martian surface exploration, transforming fragmented NASA planetary data into an actionable, terrain-aware 3D mission planner."

MARSWALK, developed by Team Epistemic Order, is an interactive 3D Martian exploration and decision-support platform designed to transform planetary data into meaningful exploration insights. It integrates information from NASA datasets, including MOLA, HiRISE, CTX, CRISM and THEMIS, to support Martian terrain visualization and scientific exploration.

Featuring an interactive Mars environment and a Traverse Mission Planner, MARSWALK enables users to explore regions such as Jezero Crater and evaluate potential routes using terrain parameters like elevation, slope and distance.

Its five key innovations are Autonomous Science Discovery, Human Mobility Estimation, Returnability Intelligence, Habitat Selection and the Mission Confidence Engine. Together, these capabilities aim to support scientific target identification, terrain-aware mobility assessment, return-route evaluation, potential habitat analysis and uncertainty-aware decision-making.

MARSWALK aims to bridge the gap between planetary mapping and practical exploration planning, providing a scalable foundation for future human exploration of Mars.
details:
1. What does the project do and how does it work? MARSWALK (Martian Astronaut Route & Scientific Exploration Planner) is a planetary exploration and mission-planning platform designed to make Martian surface exploration more informed and efficient. It brings together planetary terrain information, scientific datasets and route-planning capabilities in a unified 3D environment.

The application allows users to explore the Martian surface, navigate regions such as Jezero Crater, visualize terrain information and evaluate potential exploration routes. Its approach combines topographic information, orbital imagery and scientific observations to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the Martian environment.

The system follows three major stages:

  • Foundation: Integrates planetary information from sources such as NASA PDS, USGS, MOLA and HiRISE.
  • Processing: Uses digital elevation model (DEM) processing, local caching and coordinate-aware overlays to organize and align terrain information.
  • Output: Presents the processed information through 3D planetary visualization and mission-planning insights.

2. What benefits does it provide? MARSWALK aims to reduce the complexity of interpreting fragmented planetary information by bringing multiple data sources into one environment.

Its key benefits include:

  • Unified visualization of different Martian planetary datasets.
  • Better understanding of elevation, terrain variations and surface characteristics.
  • Terrain-aware evaluation of potential exploration routes.
  • Support for identifying scientifically interesting exploration locations.
  • Consideration of return-route planning rather than focusing only on the outbound journey.
  • Greater transparency through the identification of uncertainty in available data.
  • A modular architecture that can be extended with additional datasets and analytical capabilities.

3. What is the intended impact? The intended impact of MARSWALK is to contribute towards more intelligent and informed planetary exploration planning.

By connecting scientific observations with terrain visualization and route evaluation, the platform aims to help researchers, mission planners and future exploration teams understand the Martian environment more effectively.

In the long term, MARSWALK could provide a foundation for advanced human exploration decision-support systems, helping prioritize scientific targets, evaluate potential traverses and identify candidate locations for exploration bases.

It is intended as a planning and decision-support platform, not a certified astronaut navigation or safety system.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware or software were used? The project uses planetary datasets and software-based development tools to build its exploration environment.

Scientific data sources:

  • NASA Planetary Data System (PDS)
  • Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA)
  • High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE)
  • Context Camera (CTX)
  • Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars (CRISM)
  • Thermal Emission Imaging System (THEMIS)
  • United States Geological Survey (USGS) planetary resources

Technical components:

  • Digital Elevation Model (DEM) processing.
  • 3D planetary visualization.
  • Coordinate-aware data overlays.
  • Local data caching.
  • Terrain-based route evaluation and visualization.

AI tools were used to assist with project coding. The project's ideation, innovation, system logic, deployment approach and scalability planning were carried out by the team.

5. How is the project creative and innovative? MARSWALK introduces five core innovations that extend its purpose beyond basic planetary mapping:

  1. Autonomous Science Discovery Engine: Designed to identify and rank potentially valuable scientific exploration targets using available planetary science information.
  2. Human Mobility & Fatigue Estimator: Estimates movement time and physical effort using terrain-related factors such as slope and distance.
  3. Returnability Intelligence: Evaluates potential independent return routes, making the return journey an important part of exploration planning.
  4. Dynamic Habitat & Exploration Base Selection: Analyses terrain characteristics to identify potentially suitable locations for establishing exploration bases or habitat sites.
  5. Mission Confidence Engine: Highlights uncertainty in planetary data and derived assessments, helping users understand the reliability of available information.

The creative aspect of MARSWALK lies in combining planetary visualization, scientific information and exploration-planning concepts into one unified platform rather than treating them as separate tasks.

6. What factors did the team consider? During the project's design and development, the team considered several important factors:

  • Terrain elevation and slope: Understanding elevation changes and avoiding unnecessarily difficult terrain.
  • Surface characteristics: Using available orbital imagery and scientific observations to understand the Martian environment.
  • Route distance and mobility: Considering more than just the shortest distance when evaluating potential exploration routes.
  • Returnability: Including the possibility of a return journey in exploration planning.
  • Scientific importance: Considering the potential scientific value of exploration targets.
  • Habitat suitability: Evaluating terrain characteristics when identifying candidate base locations.
  • Data reliability: Distinguishing original scientific observations from derived calculations and simulated estimates.
  • Dataset coverage and resolution: Recognizing that different planetary datasets have different levels of detail and geographical coverage.
  • Scalability: Designing a modular architecture that can accommodate additional datasets and capabilities.

Ultimately, MARSWALK aims to transform scattered Martian scientific information into a unified, understandable and practical exploration-planning environment.
